LanguageData.STG.Tut.P1.Title: 1. The sky over this world
LanguageData.STG.Tut.P1.Body:
These stars came out of the seed this world was generated from. **Every world has its own sky, and within one world it never changes.**

The middle of the disc is straight overhead, the rim is the horizon. North is up.

Leave the window open and the sky really does turn — colony time is still running.
LanguageData.STG.Tut.P2.Title: 2. Latitude decides what you see
LanguageData.STG.Tut.P2.Body:
Which stars are up depends on **where you are standing**. The settlement's own latitude and longitude are used.

Far north, the southern stars never rise at all, while the ones near the pole never set and circle all day. At the equator the whole sky passes over you.

Move the gravship and the latitude changes with it, so the sky changes too. Seasons shift it as well: the same hour looks different a quadrum later.
LanguageData.STG.Tut.P3.Title: 3. Joining the dots
LanguageData.STG.Tut.P3.Body:
Some constellations already carry names, drawn in blue. Those came from this world's seed as well.

Press **Trace a constellation** and click stars in order. Three of them make a constellation. Clicking the last one again takes it back.

Name it and it joins the list on the right. Constellations belong to the **world**, not to the telescope, so they survive the telescope being destroyed or the colony moving on.
LanguageData.STG.Tut.P4.Title: 4. Some nights show you nothing
LanguageData.STG.Tut.P4.Body:
In daylight only the brightest few are left, and rain or snow takes away more. The stars have not gone anywhere — you simply cannot see them.

Come back on a clear night. If you would rather use this as a chart than as a telescope, the settings let you ignore weather and daylight.

With Odyssey installed you will also see what is in orbit — asteroids, platforms, a gravship on its way somewhere. Above the atmosphere there is no horizon, so the whole sky fits on the disc at once.
